Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette:
Keanu, a 53-year-old airline pilot of Oceania descent, had always prided himself on his calm demeanour and unwavering focus, qualities essential for his demanding profession. For over three decades, he had navigated the world's skies with confidence, a stability that extended to his marriage and family life. Yet, in the last five years, since a harrowing layover in a politically unstable region where he was captured and subjected to torture, his world had become increasingly fraught with an insidious, unpredictable dread. He had been held in a cramped, unsanitary room with several others, the air thick with the smell of stale fear and unwashed bodies, punctuated by the muffled cries of fellow captives and the erratic, often violent, behaviour of his captors. The moments of absolute silence, broken only by the drip of water, were the most terrifying, signaling imminent brutality.

Now, even the most mundane aspects of his life could plunge him back into that nightmare. A child's sudden cry in an airport terminal, for example, could instantly shatter his composure, acting as a potent trigger that would flood his mind with the vivid, photographic recall of the torture chamber, complete with the sickening, metallic olfactory recall of the room's specific stench. When these memories returned, so overwhelming was the accompanying rush of emotion that Keanu often had to stop whatever he was doing, his professional duties sometimes interrupted by the sheer force of the recollection.

This intense reliving of the past, particularly the precise visual and sensory details of his captivity, made Keanu hyper-vigilant in his present. The constant, gnawing sense of threat he carried, a certainty that danger lurked just beneath the surface of everyday life, made him exquisitely sensitive to new triggers. He found himself scanning crowds with an almost obsessive intensity, feeling that the very presence of many people, much like in his cell, signaled imminent harm. This pervasive sense of threat caused even seemingly innocuous situations to immediately register as potential triggers; a sudden quiet in the cockpit, a moment of unusual silence, would instantly make him feel that something dangerous was about to happen.

His heightened internal state meant that Keanu's triggers were no longer just external events. The very vividness of his memories, especially their photographic clarity, primed him to perceive certain situations as dangerous, even when they were benign. The constant internal replay made him acutely attuned to any hint of similar circumstances, transforming innocent sounds or sights into potent triggers. Consequently, the moment he encountered a crowded place, like the bustling gate before a flight, or witnessed people misbehaving, such as a passenger arguing with a flight attendant, he immediately felt an intense surge of threat, convinced that the chaos would escalate into something dangerous and uncontrollable.

At home, this threat manifested as an obsessive need for security. Keanu repeatedly checked that all doors and windows were locked, sometimes several times an hour, certain that his home was vulnerable. On flights, he found himself watching other people closely for any sign that they might harm him, his gaze lingering on passengers, trying to decipher their intentions, a habit that became increasingly isolating. His co-pilot once remarked on his unusual quietness, unaware of the internal battle raging. The accumulation of these experiences had started to impact his work; while he never compromised safety, the mental exhaustion was immense, making him dread his shifts. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that his suffering had permanently altered him, a terrifying prospect for a man whose life depended on clear judgment. It was this fear of losing control, of his internal world finally overriding his external competence, that finally compelled him to seek help.
